query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy, the anomalous stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior observed at elevated temperatures (600°C–1200°C) are due to a transition from a screw dislocation–dominated deformation mechanism at room temperature to an edge dislocation–dominated mechanism at high temperatures. This shift is mediated by temperature‐induced local lattice distortions that activate alternative slip modes.
generation.material_initial_state: Fully homogenized, cold-rolled and annealed HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting a disordered BCC solid-solution structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Systematic high-temperature mechanical testing combined with in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and dilatometry, conducted in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at controlled temperatures from 600°C to 1200°C, with fixed strain rates and under inert gas to avoid oxidation, compared against room temperature baseline measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced local lattice distortions that facilitate a slip mode transition from screw-dominated to edge-dominated dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, deformation is controlled by screw dislocations. As the temperature increases, thermal activation reduces the energy barrier for edge dislocation motion, enabling a transition that results in a plateau in yield strength and modifies both thermal expansion and elastic responses due to the altered dislocation dynamics and lattice distortions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the room temperature baseline, the alloy will exhibit a noticeable decrease in yield strength with increasing temperature until the activation of edge dislocations leads to a plateau in strength, accompanied by measurable changes in elastic moduli and thermal expansion coefficients. In-situ diffraction is expected to reveal evidence of altered lattice distortion patterns consistent with increased edge dislocation activity.
generation.baseline: Room temperature mechanical properties and lattice structure characterized by dominant screw dislocation behavior and relatively higher yield strength.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for tests performed in the temperature range from 600°C to 1200°C under inert atmosphere conditions with a constant strain rate.
generation.uncertainty: While previous evidence supports a dislocation slip mode transition in similar refractory high-entropy alloys, the exact quantitative changes in yield strength, elastic moduli, and thermal expansion in HfNbTaTiZr as a function of temperature are not precisely predicted. There is also uncertainty in the degree to which local lattice distortions modulate these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples subjected to identical homogenization and cold work processes. Conduct baseline mechanical tests (stress–strain, dilatometry, and XRD) at room temperature, then perform in-situ high-temperature tensile tests in a controlled inert atmosphere at incrementally increasing temperatures from 600°C to 1200°C while simultaneously monitoring lattice structure and dislocation characteristics using synchrotron X-ray diffraction and post-mortem TEM analyses.
measurements: Yield strength and plasticity as a function of temperature
Elastic moduli and lattice parameter changes via in-situ XRD
Characterization of dislocation structures (screw vs. edge) via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature tests do not reveal a distinct transition in dislocation behavior (i.e., no evidence for increased edge dislocation activity or altered lattice distortion patterns) and if the yield strength/elastic moduli do not exhibit a plateau behavior within 600°C–1200°C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). AbstractThere is a strong demand for materials with inherently high creep resistance in the harsh environment of next-generation nuclear reactors. High entropy alloys have drawn intense attention in this regard due to their excellent elevated temperature properties and irradiation resistance. Here, the time-dependent plastic deformation behavior of two refractory high entropy alloys was investigated, namely HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr. These alloys are based on reduced activity metals from the 4-5-6 elemental palette that would allow easy post-service recycling after use in nuclear reactors. The creep behavior was investigated using nano-indentation over the temperature range of 298 K to 573 K under static and dynamic loads up to 5 N. Creep stress exponent for HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr was found to be in the range of 20–140 and the activation volume was ~16–20b3, indicating dislocation dominated mechanism. The stress exponent increased with increasing indentation depth due to a higher density of dislocations and their entanglement at larger depth and the exponent decreased with increasing temperature due to thermally activated dislocations. Refractory Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW RHEAs with ultra-high temperature strength have been designed using high-melting-point elements and verified by the solid-solution strengthening theory. After homogenization treatment at 2100°C for 2 h with subsequent air cooling, the RHEAs reveal no composition segregation and precipitates. The HfMoNbTaW in the as-homogenized state provides the highest elevated-temperature yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600 °C.
